items.title: What AI Skills Do Employers Actually Look For in 2026?
items.summary: Data from the National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE) shows that more than one-third of entry-level jobs now require AI competency—nearly triple the share from fall 2025—with over half of these postings falling outside of traditional IT into fields like marketing, operations, and business analytics.

items.title: New grads have to compete with AI for entry
items.summary: A survey of 1,000 U.S. hiring managers revealed that 48% would rather invest in AI tools than hire and train a recent college graduate, forcing business majors to demonstrate both strong foundational workplace readiness and AI fluency to remain competitive.

items.title: How AI is Reshaping Business Administration Degree Careers in 2026
items.summary: As AI automates routine corporate administrative and forecasting tasks, business administration graduates are increasingly expected to specialize in strategic data analysis, change management, and hybrid roles like "AI Business Analysts" to bridge the gap between technical teams and operations.

items.title: After Years of Cuts, Employers Say They're Ready to Hire More Entry-Level Workers Again as AI Use Evolves
items.summary: Following a difficult era of automated task displacement, new NACE Spring Update data shows a projected 5.6% increase in hiring for the Class of 2026 as employers look to bring on graduates capable of actively integrating and coordinating AI systems across corporate frameworks.

items.title: Key Things to Know About AI, Automation, and the Future of Health Studies Degree Careers
items.summary: Over 40% of health studies employers have already integrated AI tools, creating a job market where graduates who possess advanced digital literacy and AI fluency earn up to a 15% salary premium.

items.title: How AI Will Transform the Healthcare Workforce in 2026
items.summary: Rapid clinical AI adoption has outpaced formal training programs, making AI governance and human-AI collaboration a key point of negotiation in the healthcare labor market as nearly half of all nurses now utilize AI on the job.

items.title: Safe from AI: which jobs will help you thrive in the future?
items.summary: Routine health-related administrative and pharmacy support jobs are highly vulnerable to AI integration, while clinical prescribing professionals (doctors, nurses, pharmacists) remain highly secure because they bear the final ethical responsibility for patient treatment.

items.title: Will AI Replace Healthcare Jobs? Not How You May Think
items.summary: AI is shifting the job market for health professionals away from documentation and medical coding toward roles focused on high-stakes human connection, fine motor skills, and complex decision-making.

items.title: Cedars-Sinai CDAO: Meaningful AI deployment cannot wait
items.summary: Healthcare systems are aggressively deploying AI as a productivity multiplier to help existing clinicians cope with severe labor shortages and reengineer care delivery systems.

items.title: The state of the creative industry 2026: what our survey tells us about pay, burnout and AI
items.summary: A global survey of nearly 900 creative professionals revealed that while 86% of respondents are actively using AI tools in their work, only 10% believe the technology's overall impact on the creative industry is positive, with many reporting increased career anxiety and high rates of burnout.

items.title: Visual artists are in an AI crisis, this new survey explains why: L.A. arts and culture this weekend
items.summary: Drawing on a landmark Carnegie Mellon University study of verified professional visual artists, this report details how 99% of those surveyed dislike generative AI, voicing critical concerns that employers and clients are driving down human wages by settling for "good enough" AI-generated alternatives.

items.title: AI Won’t Replace Artists
items.summary: This piece analyzes the shifting labor economics of creative careers, arguing that AI has commodified the cheap "draft layer" (such as storyboards and concept variations), forcing art graduates to move up the value chain into roles that emphasize high-stakes taste, brand-defining design leadership, and rights assurance.

items.title: AI Is Changing Creative Work, but the Arts Aren't Disappearing
items.summary: Analyzing national workforce and labor data, this report finds that while generative AI has not yet caused broad declines in artists' overall earnings, it is heavily shifting early-stage creative workflows, with many artists now frequently using AI tools to brainstorm, organize tasks, and quickly experiment with new ideas.

items.title: AI, Automation, and the Future of Liberal Arts Degree Careers
items.summary: This report outlines how the integration of AI is creating hybrid career opportunities for liberal arts graduates, showcasing emerging pathways like "AI Ethics Specialists" who combine training in philosophy, law, and social implications to define boundaries for machine-learning systems.

items.title: Why AI is ‘resurrecting’ the liberal arts for the Class of 2026
items.summary: Career development experts highlight that because AI has commodified execution-level technical tasks, the market is experiencing a reversal in value that highly favors the "liberal arts brain" for its emphasis on strategic intent, critical thinking, and ethical oversight.

items.title: AI, Automation, and the Future of Humanities Degree Careers
items.summary: This analysis explores how AI-driven content automation is shifting employment demands, pushing humanities graduates to adapt by focusing on specialized, high-growth areas like digital humanities and ethical AI development where digital literacy and narrative strategy are prized.

items.title: Revenge of the Communicators: HR Teams Are Suddenly Scrambling for Good Liberal Arts Talent
items.summary: This piece reports on a quiet hiring surge across industries (from tech startups to entertainment giants) that are doubling down on communications and liberal arts majors because of AI's inability to replicate nuanced, human-centric internal storytelling and brand narrative strategies.

items.title: AI Impact on Student Career Choices: Survey Reveals 4 in 10 Rethinking College Majors
items.summary: Driven by anxieties over automation, nearly 40% of college students are reconsidering their majors, prompting a significant drop in raw computer science enrollments and a notable shift toward "AI-resistant" or hybrid fields that leverage irreplaceable human elements, such as the social sciences, complex problem-solving, and empathy.

items.title: AI, Automation, and the Future of Sociology and Political Science Careers
items.summary: While basic data entry and routine reporting in the social sciences face high automation risks, overall hiring for social researchers with AI expertise is projected to rise 15% over the next decade as roughly 45% of political and sociological roles now require proficiency in AI-assisted data interpretation.

items.title: AI and the Labor Market: Revolution or Evolution?
items.summary: This labor market analysis reveals that fields like the humanities and social sciences—which prioritize interpretation, ethics, and human context—are highly resilient, though social science graduates are strongly encouraged to pick up complementary tech skills to qualify for the surging number of "AI-ready" job postings.

items.title: GovAI Opportunities 2026: Apply for Research, AI Policy, Chief of Staff and Operations Roles with Salaries Up to $205,000
items.summary: The rapid deployment of advanced machine learning models is creating high-paying, non-technical jobs in AI governance, safety, and regulation (with salaries up to $205,000), actively recruiting social science backgrounds to tackle geopolitical risks, ethical guidelines, and public policy frameworks.

items.title: College graduates face competitive market as artificial intelligence spending rises
items.summary: A new survey highlights a tightening entry-level market, showing that nearly half of hiring managers are choosing to redirect recruitment funds to invest in AI tools rather than train new graduates, meaning STEM applicants must demonstrate immediate technical competency and strong soft skills to get hired.

items.title: Top STEM Jobs for AI Career Advancement
items.summary: While 88% of organizations have integrated AI, a severe skills gap persists, offering high-paying premiums for STEM grads who can master AI/ML, data science, and "AI workflow specialist" roles that connect intelligent systems to business operations.

items.title: What types of AI jobs are emerging for new college graduates?
items.summary: This report outlines that 35% of all entry-level job postings now specifically require AI-related skills, fueling demand for STEM majors in emerging pathways like AI data curation, AI ethics, and ethical AI development.

items.title: Class of 2026: Young college graduates and AI-exposed occupations
items.summary: Data analyzing the newest graduating class indicates that although STEM majors are highly exposed to AI tools in their daily careers, this exposure is not driving a displacement of young tech workers but is instead requiring them to act as the direct operators of AI systems.

items.title: Why the liberal arts can help young Americans prepare for the era of AI
items.summary: Career experts suggest that as AI automates highly technical skills like coding, employers are increasingly valuing the emotional intelligence (EQ), critical thinking, and versatile communication skills fostered by a traditional liberal arts education.

items.title: New grads have to compete with AI for entry
items.summary: A survey shows that nearly half of U.S. hiring managers would rather invest in AI tools than hire and train a recent college graduate, elevating the bar for entry-level candidates who must quickly master workplace communication and AI-collaboration skills.

items.title: Students Pivot Majors as AI Reshapes Higher Education Landscape
items.summary: A landmark Gallup-Lumina study indicates that over 40% of college students have seriously considered changing their majors due to AI disruption, driving fresh enrollment interest toward "AI-resistant" paths that highlight empathy, complex human problem-solving, and hands-on skills.

items.title: How AI Is Changing Skilled Trades in 2026 (Your Job Is Safer Than You Think)
items.summary: The rapid expansion of AI is driving an unprecedented surge in demand for hands-on trade majors—such as electricians, pipefitters, and HVAC technicians—who are essential for constructing and cooling the massive physical data center infrastructure that powers AI systems.

items.title: AI Reshapes U.S. Job Market: Blue-Collar Workers Poised to Gain as White-Collar Hiring Slows
items.summary: As generative AI automates routine cognitive tasks and cools down corporate, entry-level white-collar hiring, a major shift is redirecting the labor market toward highly secure, well-paying trade roles requiring physical dexterity and manual problem-solving.

items.title: AI Blue-Collar Job Shift
items.summary: Major industrial and telecom employers like Ford and AT&T are ramping up recruitment of trade majors—including mechanics, technicians, and electricians—to support hardware-heavy initiatives like 5G rollouts and electric vehicle manufacturing that are immune to AI automation.
